title: Canada GP 2026: Practice, Sprint Qualifying Analysis & Weekend Predictions
summary: Mercedes turned a single Friday practice session into a statement of intent, locking out the FP1 aggregated order before converting it into a sprint qualifying front-row lockout in Montreal. Our exclusive aggregated-vs-actual lap analysis reveals McLaren sitting on the weekend's biggest untapped potential, while the Ferraris quietly delivered near-perfect single laps. Here is the data behind the headlines, and our bold predictions for the sprint and the main event.

sections.heading: FP1 Recap: The Data Behind the Dominance
sections.content:
On a sprint weekend there is no hiding place. One sixty-minute session is all the teams get before the timesheets start to matter, and at Circuit Gilles Villeneuve it was Mercedes who used it best. Kimi Antonelli topped the FP1 aggregated standings with a theoretical best of 1:13.402, with George Russell right alongside him at 1:13.544, just 0.142 adrift. Two silver cars clear of the field after a single hour is exactly the kind of signal our aggregated data is built to surface.

The aggregated figure stitches together each driver's personal best Sector 1, Sector 2 and Sector 3 from across the whole session, regardless of which lap they came from. It is the truest read of ultimate pace available anywhere, and it is not published on F1.com or any official source. In Antonelli's case there was nothing to stitch: his best aggregated lap and his fastest actual lap were one and the same 1:13.402, every sector landing on lap 26. That is a teenager putting the entire lap together on command.

Behind the Mercedes pair, the picture tightened dramatically. Lewis Hamilton led the chasing pack on 1:14.176, shading Charles Leclerc (1:14.287), Max Verstappen (1:14.366), Lando Norris (1:14.407) and Oscar Piastri (1:14.460). Just over a quarter of a second separated third from seventh, which on a sprint weekend with no second practice to fall back on is a genuinely nervy place to be.

What the aggregated data predicted, sprint qualifying largely confirmed. Mercedes converted their Friday morning edge into a front-row lockout hours later, and the McLaren duo who looked merely mid-pack on raw FP1 lap time surged forward exactly as their sector potential suggested they could. The only practice session of the weekend told us almost everything we needed to know.

sections.heading: Understanding Aggregated vs Actual Times
sections.content:
If you only follow the official timesheets, you see the actual times - the fastest single, complete lap each driver managed, all three sectors strung together on the same tour. That is what F1.com shows. Our aggregated figure does something different and, for predicting qualifying, more powerful: it takes a driver's best Sector 1, best Sector 2 and best Sector 3 from anywhere in the session and adds them together to reveal the lap they are genuinely capable of.

Why does that predict qualifying better? Because when it counts in Q3, drivers do exactly this - they nail every sector on one lap. A small delta between aggregated and actual means a driver is already extracting everything and is unlikely to find much more. A large delta means there is real lap time still locked away, waiting to be unleashed when the pressure is on. It is the single best early-warning system for who is about to step up.

That is precisely the story of this Friday. Antonelli, Russell, Hamilton and Verstappen all posted deltas of essentially zero - they were already maximised. The McLarens, by contrast, carried deltas of +0.392 (Norris) and +0.503 (Piastri), the biggest in the top order. The data was effectively flashing a warning that the papaya cars had more to give. Hold that thought for the sprint qualifying section.

sections.heading: Sprint Qualifying: Russell Snatches Sprint Pole
sections.content:
George Russell delivered when it mattered, banking a 1:12.965 in SQ3 to take sprint pole and turn the FP1 form on its head between team-mates. Antonelli, fastest in the morning, had to settle for second on 1:13.033 - a margin of just 0.068. An all-Mercedes front row in Montreal, and a reminder that on this low-downforce, traction-and-braking circuit the Silver Arrows have found something special.

The McLaren resurgence our aggregated data forecast arrived right on cue. Norris (1:13.280) and Piastri (1:13.299) locked out the second row, both leaping clear of where their raw FP1 lap times had placed them - exactly the upside those chunky FP1 deltas had promised. Splitting them from the Mercedes was a slender margin, setting up a four-team fight at the front for the sprint.

Ferrari were the quiet story. Hamilton (1:13.326) edged Leclerc (1:13.410) for fifth, the pair separated by under a tenth and never quite finding the final flourish to trouble the top four. Verstappen, meanwhile, dragged a Red Bull that has looked a handful all weekend up to seventh on 1:13.504 - arguably one of the laps of the session given the car beneath him. Isack Hadjar impressed in the sister car for eighth (1:13.605).

The surprises came at the edges of the top ten. Rookie Arvid Lindblad put his Racing Bulls ninth (1:13.737), a standout effort, while Carlos Sainz scraped into SQ3 in tenth but was over eight tenths off Lindblad at 1:14.536. The big casualty was Audi's Nico Hulkenberg, eliminated in SQ2 in eleventh despite topping the midfield in FP1 - a costly slip on a weekend with no margin for error.

sections.heading: Sector-by-Sector Breakdown
sections.content:
Montreal rewards a very particular blend: punchy traction out of slow chicanes, stability under heavy braking, and the confidence to skim the walls through the final sector. Breaking FP1 down by sector shows exactly where Mercedes built their advantage - and it was comprehensive.

In Sector 1, the run down to and through the opening corners, Antonelli was untouchable at 20.785, with Russell next on 20.896 and Hamilton a close third at 20.910. That is a Mercedes one-three in the section most dependent on power delivery and braking stability, and a clear sign the W17 is hooked up where this lap is won. Sector 2 told the same tale: Russell led the way at 23.224, with Antonelli (23.330) and Norris a surprising third (23.400) showing the McLaren's strength in the medium-speed transitions.

The final sector, the technical run to the wall of champions and the start-finish straight, again belonged to Mercedes. Antonelli's 29.287 was the benchmark, with Russell (29.424) and Verstappen (29.558) chasing. Notably, this is where the Ferraris leaked time - Hamilton's 29.772 and Leclerc's 29.692 were among the weaker S3 efforts of the front-runners, hinting at a car that is strong on entry but a touch nervous on exit traction.

Stitch the theoretical best sectors together and the conclusion is unavoidable: Mercedes own the fastest Sector 1 (Antonelli), the fastest Sector 2 (Russell) and the fastest Sector 3 (Antonelli). When one team holds the optimum in all three sectors, the front-row lockout in sprint qualifying stops being a surprise and starts looking inevitable.

sections.heading: Tyre Strategy Analysis
sections.content:
Sprint weekends compress everything, and tyre management on Friday becomes a chess match played with a limited allocation. The dominant compound pattern across FP1 was a single soft run for a representative lap backed up by hard-tyre running for longer stints - the textbook approach when you have only one session to learn the circuit and gather race data simultaneously.

The leading teams were disciplined. Mercedes, Ferrari, Red Bull and Piastri's McLaren all logged one soft and one hard in FP1, then leaned heavily on the medium through sprint qualifying, where most front-runners used two medium sets to bank a banker lap before going again. That medium-heavy SQ approach is telling: it suggests the teams trust the medium as a viable sprint-race compound and want to preserve softs for the main qualifying hour.

Norris stands out as the strategic outlier, burning through three hard sets in FP1 alone and racking up the highest soft count of the weekend by main qualifying. That points to McLaren chasing setup answers harder than anyone - consistent with those big FP1 deltas - and being willing to spend rubber to find them. At the other extreme, Alex Albon's tally is strikingly low (just three sets through qualifying), a conservative, preserve-everything approach from Williams.

For the sprint itself, expect the medium to be the weapon of choice for a flat-out, no-stop dash. The hard becomes the main-race tyre for the longer Sunday run, with softs reserved for the qualifying shootout. Given how little long-run data anyone gathered in a single FP1, degradation will be the great unknown - and the team that read their limited Friday running best will have a decisive edge.

sections.heading: Key Findings and Surprises
sections.content:
1. Mercedes are the team to beat. They topped the FP1 aggregated order one-two, owned the theoretical best in all three sectors, and converted it into a sprint qualifying front-row lockout. Russell (sprint pole, 1:12.965) and Antonelli (1:13.033) are operating on a different level around Montreal this weekend.

2. McLaren were the overperformers, exactly as the data warned. Norris (+0.392) and Piastri (+0.503) carried the biggest aggregated-vs-actual deltas in FP1, signposting hidden pace - and both duly leapt to the second row in sprint qualifying. This is the aggregated methodology working as designed.

3. The midfield order is brutally tight. Lindblad's ninth on debut-season form (1:13.737) was a standout, while Hadjar continues to make the second Red Bull look respectable in eighth. Audi were the weekend's biggest disappointment so far: Hulkenberg led the midfield in FP1 but fell in SQ2, a reminder of how unforgiving a one-practice format can be.

4. Ferrari are quietly in the mix but vulnerable in Sector 3. Hamilton and Leclerc posted near-perfect single laps in FP1 (deltas of +0.000 and +0.068), so there is little hidden upside to come - what you see is roughly what they have, and their final-sector traction looks like the weak link.

5. The notable data anomaly: Franco Colapinto registered no representative FP1 lap (a null entry across the board), having only completed limited running. He is absent from the practice tables but bounced back to make SQ2, classified thirteenth - proof of how much can still be salvaged from a compromised Friday.

sections.heading: Sprint Race Predictions
sections.content:
Sprint Podium Prediction:
1. George Russell (Mercedes) - Sprint pole, the fastest car, and clean air into Turn 1. Track position is everything around a circuit where overtaking is tough, and Russell holds the keys.
2. Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes) - Right on his team-mate's gearbox all weekend. Expect a tense intra-Mercedes opening lap, but the pace to follow Russell home is clearly there.
3. Lando Norris (McLaren) - The papaya pace is real and trending upward. From P3 he is perfectly placed to capitalise on any Mercedes wobble.

Sprint Strategy: A flat-out, no-stop dash on the medium compound for the leaders, who banked their medium sets precisely for this. Expect the front-runners to manage the rears out of the slow corners over the closing laps rather than chase outright lap time.

Sprint Wildcard: Max Verstappen from P7. If he gets a clean launch and the first-lap chaos breaks his way, he has the racecraft to be a top-five threat in a car that is plainly not the class of the field.

Key Sprint Battle: The McLaren-versus-Ferrari fight for the final podium step. Norris and Piastri start ahead, but Hamilton and Leclerc on similar tyres will be all over their gearboxes if the papaya cars lose temperature.

sections.heading: Qualifying & Race Day Predictions
sections.content:
Qualifying Prediction (based on FP1 aggregated pace): The aggregated data is unambiguous - Mercedes have the fastest theoretical lap by a clear margin. Expect a pole in the 1:12.6–1:12.9 window as the track rubbers in, with Antonelli and Russell again separated by a hair. Watch the McLarens closely: those large FP1 deltas mean Norris and Piastri have untapped lap time the aggregated figure has already exposed, and they are the most likely to gatecrash the front row. Predicted top three for the main qualifying: Russell, Antonelli, Norris.

Race Prediction: This becomes a track-position and tyre-degradation game. With so little long-run data from a single FP1, the team that best preserves its rears over a stint wins. We are backing a one-stop on the hard-to-medium order for most of the grid, with an undercut threat keeping the leaders honest.

Podium Prediction:
1. George Russell (Mercedes)
2. Lando Norris (McLaren)
3. Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes)

Wildcard Factors: Montreal is a safety-car magnet - the Wall of Champions and tight chicanes guarantee debris and incidents. A well-timed caution could flip the strategy entirely and hand the lead to whoever pits at the right moment. Late-afternoon weather is the other variable to monitor.

Dark Horse: Oscar Piastri. His FP1 delta of +0.503 was the largest of any front-runner, meaning there is more in his pocket than the timesheets suggest. If McLaren unlock it in qualifying, he is a genuine race-winner.

Key Battle to Watch: The intra-Mercedes duel. Russell versus Antonelli for outright supremacy is the story of the weekend - team-mates separated by hundredths, one a proven race-winner, the other a rising star unwilling to play second fiddle. How Mercedes manage that on a circuit where the lead car controls the race could define their Sunday.
